items.prompt: Dana's manager quotes a raise as '+5.6% on base.' Per this unit, what's the problem with using that number alone to judge whether the offer is fair?
choices: 5.6% is too small a number to matter
It ignores bonus and equity, which don't move the same way base does
Raises should always be quoted in dollars, never percentages
It's mathematically incorrect
items.explanation: Total comp is base + bonus + equity, and the three components behave differently year to year — a base-only percentage is accurate about one component and silent about the other two, which is exactly what hid Dana's equity cliff.
items.reference:
💵 Base — fixed, usually flat or small annual bump
🎯 Bonus — scales with base, but never guaranteed
📈 Equity — vests in tranches, can hit $0 without a refresher

Why: a raise percentage on base alone answers a real but narrow question — it says nothing about the other two-thirds of the picture.
items.learnMore:
Total comp has three components

Base, bonus, and equity each behave differently year to year. Judging fairness from base alone hides the two components most likely to swing sharply — bonus can drop to 0%, and equity can vest to $0 the moment a grant runs out.

items.prompt: The market band for Dana's role runs P25 $150,000 to P90 $230,000, with P50 at $175,000. What does it mean that Dana's raise offer of $179,000 sits 'just above P50'?
choices: Her offer is a below-market outlier
Half the market for this role/level/location pays less than $179,000, and the other half pays more
$179,000 is exactly the median regardless of the band's shape
P50 means the 50th highest-paid person in the company
items.explanation: P50 (the median) means half the reported data points for that role/level/location fall below it and half fall above — landing just above P50 means Dana's offer is roughly typical, slightly on the higher side of typical, not exceptional and not below-market.
items.reference:

Why: a percentile tells you where a number ranks against real market data — a raw dollar figure alone can't tell you that.
items.learnMore:
Percentile, not raw size

A market band reports percentiles (P25, P50, P75, P90) of what people in a comparable role, level, and location actually get paid. Where a number falls in that range is the signal — a dollar figure that 'sounds like a lot' in isolation can still be below market.

items.prompt: Per this unit, why does Dana check three independent sources (a leveling site, a comp-survey summary, and a recruiter's stated range) instead of trusting just one?
choices: Because it's required by law before negotiating
Because no single source is fully reliable alone, and agreement across sources builds real confidence
Because recruiters always lie about pay ranges
Because self-reported data is always more accurate than surveys
items.explanation: Each source has a real weakness — self-reported data lacks verification, formal surveys are hard to access directly, and a single recruiter's range is one data point with its own incentive to anchor low. Cross-checking multiple sources is what makes the resulting band trustworthy.

🌐 Leveling site — large sample, self-reported, unverified
📑 Comp survey — verified, employer-submitted, access-gated
🧑‍💼 Recruiter range — real and current, but one data point

Why: each source has a distinct weakness — cross-checking multiple sources is what turns a guess into real market data.
items.learnMore:
No single source is enough

Aggregated self-reported bands, formal comp surveys, and recruiter-stated ranges each have a real strength and a real weakness. Checking them against each other is what makes the resulting picture trustworthy enough to negotiate from.

items.prompt: Dana's original grant is 4,000 RSUs vesting 1,000/year over 4 years. This is the 4th and final year of that grant, and no refresher has been offered. What happens to her equity tranche next year?
choices: It stays the same, $14,000, since grants renew automatically
It drops to $0, unless a new (refresher) grant is issued before then
It doubles, since the grant is fully vested
It converts automatically into extra base salary
items.explanation: A grant that finishes vesting produces no further tranches on its own — without a refresher grant issued before the original one runs out, next year's equity value is $0, which is exactly the cliff Dana's raise letter didn't mention.
items.reference:
📆 Vesting schedule — releases a grant in tranches, not all at once
⛔ Cliff — a minimum period before any shares vest at all
🔄 Refresher — a new grant issued before the old one runs out

Why: a grant that finishes vesting produces $0 in new tranches the following year unless a refresher is issued first.
items.learnMore:
Grants run out

A vesting schedule turns a grant into pay over several years, not indefinitely. Once the last tranche vests, that grant contributes $0 the following year unless a refresher grant was issued before it ran out — this is the single most commonly missed part of reading an equity-heavy offer.

items.prompt: What is a 'refresher grant,' per this unit?
choices: A bonus paid in cash instead of stock
A new equity grant issued before the original grant finishes vesting, so total comp doesn't drop to $0 the year the original runs out
A grant that replaces base salary entirely
The final tranche of an existing grant
items.explanation: A refresher grant is a new grant layered in before the original one finishes vesting — its purpose is specifically to prevent the cliff that happens when a multi-year grant runs its course with nothing lined up to replace it.

items.prompt: Fernbank is a private company. Why can't its equity be valued the same simple way as Anchorline's (public) stock?
choices: Private companies never grant equity to engineers
Private equity has no observable market price — it's marked by a periodic 409A appraisal, usually well below the latest funding round's price, and isn't spendable until an exit event
Private equity is always worth more than public equity
409A valuations are set by the employee, not the company
items.explanation: Public stock has one observable, tradeable price today. Private equity is priced by a periodic independent appraisal (the 409A), typically below what investors paid in the last funding round, and none of it is realizable until an actual exit event — a fundamentally different kind of number.
items.reference:
Public equity

One live, tradeable price; liquid the day it vests

Private equity

409A appraisal, illiquid until an exit event, could be worth $0

Why: two equity numbers of the same dollar size are not the same risk if one is liquid and one isn't.
items.learnMore:
Current vs. grant valuation

Private-company equity is priced by an independent 409A appraisal for tax/strike purposes, distinct from what the latest funding round paid, and distinct again from any eventual IPO/acquisition price. None of it is realizable until an actual exit event — unlike public stock, which trades at one observable price today.

items.prompt: Fernbank's most recent funding round priced shares at $40, but the current 409A appraisal values them at $14. Which number should Dana use to value this year's vesting tranche, and why?
choices: The $40 round price, since it's the most recent number
The $14 409A value, since that's the independent appraisal actually used to value vesting shares for tax/comp purposes
Neither — private equity should be valued at $0 until IPO
The average of the two, $27
items.explanation: The 409A appraisal, not the last funding round's preferred-share price, is the figure used to value vesting shares — funding rounds are typically priced for preferred shares under different terms than the common shares employees hold, and are almost always higher than the 409A.

items.prompt: Per this unit's framing, what kind of question is 'is my offer fair'?
choices: A gut-feeling question, best answered by comparing to what feels like a lot of money
A market-data question, answered by gathering real comparable data and placing your number in context
An unanswerable question, since pay is always subjective
A legal question that only HR can answer
items.explanation: This unit treats fairness as answerable — through real market data (multiple sources), normalized comparison, band placement, and context adjustment — not as a matter of gut feeling or an unanswerable subjective question.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Gather data from multiple sources
2️⃣ Normalize to the same shape/window
3️⃣ Place in a real market band
4️⃣ Adjust for context (COL, liquidity, trend)

Why: fairness is answerable with a repeatable process, not a feeling — that's the whole point of doing market research before negotiating.
items.learnMore:
Fairness is a research question

This unit's whole premise is that 'is this fair' has a real, researchable answer: gather multiple data sources, normalize every offer to the same shape, place the result in a market band, then adjust for context like geography and liquidity — not a gut check against how big the number sounds.

items.prompt: Put the four-step market-research process in the correct order.
choices: Place in band → gather data → adjust for context → normalize
Gather data → normalize → place in band → adjust for context
Normalize → adjust for context → gather data → place in band
Adjust for context → gather data → place in band → normalize
items.explanation: The process runs: gather data from multiple sources, normalize every offer to the same total-comp shape and time window, place the normalized number in a real market band, then adjust for context (geography, liquidity, trend). Each step depends on the one before it.
items.reference:
1️⃣ Gather — multiple independent sources
2️⃣ Normalize — same components, same window
3️⃣ Place in band — where does it rank?
4️⃣ Adjust — geo/COL, liquidity, trend

Why: each step depends on the one before it — you can't place an un-normalized number in a band, and you can't adjust a number that hasn't been placed yet.
items.learnMore:
The four steps build on each other

Gathering data without normalizing gives you incomparable numbers. Normalizing without placing in a band gives you a number with no context. Placing in a band without adjusting for geography, liquidity, or trend gives you an incomplete picture. Each step is a prerequisite for the next.

A useful source is not the same as a sufficient one

Every source in this unit's step 1 has a real strength worth using and a real weakness worth compensating for by checking it against the others — a recruiter's range is current and specific, but shaped by the recruiter's own incentives, which is why it's one input, not the whole answer.

items.prompt: Why does normalizing every offer to 'base + target bonus + this year's vesting equity, same one-year window' matter before comparing two offers?

Because comparing offers with mismatched shapes (e.g., base-only vs. total comp, or a one-time bonus included vs. excluded) produces a misleading comparison
Because bonus and equity should always be excluded from any real comparison
Because normalization is only needed when comparing more than two offers
items.explanation: Two offers can only be fairly compared if they're expressed in the same shape and time window — comparing Fernbank's total comp against only Anchorline's base, or including a one-time signing bonus on one side and not the other, produces a gap that isn't real.
items.reference:
⚖️ Same components on both sides: base + bonus + this year's equity
🗓️ Same time window: one year, steady-state, not a signing-bonus-inflated year one

Why: a comparison is only real if both sides are shaped the same way — otherwise the 'gap' you're seeing is partly an artifact of the mismatch.
items.learnMore:
Normalize before comparing

Dana excludes Anchorline's one-time signing bonus from her steady-state comparison specifically because it doesn't repeat — including it would make year-one look like the ongoing reality when it isn't. Normalizing means matching both the components counted and the time period they cover.

Anchorline $196.7k > Fernbank $179k

COL-adjusted

Cost of living varies sharply by city, driven heavily by housing. A cost-of-living index converts a nominal salary in one city to its purchasing-power equivalent in another — turning a 'clear winner' comparison into a real trade-off with a number attached, though it isn't the whole story (career capital, team, and role scope aren't priced by a COL index).

409A-priced, illiquid, realizable only at exit — could be $0

Anchorline (public)

Live market price, tradeable the day it vests

A private company's equity is priced by an independent appraisal and can only be converted to cash at a future exit event that may never happen. A public company's stock is liquid immediately.
